title: Biotin and Alcohol: Safety, Depletion, Hair, and Lab Test Risks
excerpt: Is it safe to take biotin with alcohol? How heavy drinking affects biotin, whether it helps hangovers or hair loss, and why biotin can skew blood tests.
metaDescription: Can you take biotin with alcohol? How drinking affects biotin, whether it helps hangovers or hair loss, and why high-dose biotin can skew blood tests.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** biotin and alcohol are safe to take together. There is no known dangerous interaction between them, and taking your usual biotin supplement on a day you have a few drinks won't change how alcohol affects you. The more interesting relationships run in other directions. Long-term heavy drinking can interfere with how your gut absorbs biotin. High-dose biotin, the kind sold for hair and nails, can throw off important blood tests, including the one emergency rooms use to check for a heart attack. And despite how often it shows up in hangover and "detox" products, there is no good evidence that biotin relieves a hangover or undoes alcohol's effects on your hair or skin.

**The quick rules:** If you drink socially and eat a normal diet, you almost certainly get enough biotin and don't need extra because of alcohol. If you take a high-dose biotin supplement (5,000 to 10,000 mcg is common in hair products), tell your doctor and any lab before blood work, and tell emergency staff if you end up in urgent care with chest pain or a racing heart after a night out. If you're taking biotin hoping it will fix thinning hair or dull skin that you think is linked to drinking, cutting back on alcohol and sorting out sleep, food, and stress will usually do far more than the pill.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before taking biotin if** you take seizure medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, have thyroid disease, or have heart problems that need regular blood tests. **Tell your doctor or the lab before any blood test** if you take a biotin supplement, including multivitamins and hair, skin, and nail products. **See a doctor if** you have patchy or sudden hair loss, a red scaly rash around your eyes, nose, or mouth, numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, or lasting tiredness. In an emergency, call 911.

## Is It Safe to Take Biotin With Alcohol?

Yes, for nearly everyone. Biotin is vitamin B7, one of the water-soluble B vitamins. Your body uses it as a helper for several enzymes involved in turning food into energy, building fats, and making glucose. It isn't broken down by the same liver pathways that handle alcohol, it doesn't change your blood alcohol level, and it doesn't make alcohol more or less intoxicating.

That's different from many medications, where the concern is that alcohol and the drug compete for the same liver enzymes or add to each other's side effects. Biotin doesn't cause drowsiness, doesn't irritate the stomach the way aspirin or ibuprofen can, and doesn't put extra strain on the liver at normal doses. The US National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements, which publishes the main government fact sheet on biotin, has not set an upper limit for it because no harmful effects have been clearly shown even at high intakes. Your kidneys clear what you don't use.

So the practical answer is simple. If you take a daily multivitamin, a B-complex, or a hair, skin, and nail supplement that contains biotin, you don't need to skip it on days you drink, and you don't need to space it hours apart from a glass of wine.

There are three situations where the combination deserves more thought, and they're covered below:

1. **You drink heavily on a regular basis.** Alcohol may then lower how much biotin you absorb, along with several other nutrients.
2. **You take high-dose biotin and need blood work.** This is the risk most people don't know about.
3. **You take certain seizure medications.** Some of these lower biotin levels and also interact with alcohol on their own.

## Does Alcohol Deplete Biotin?

Heavy, long-term drinking can lower biotin levels. Occasional or moderate drinking is unlikely to make a meaningful difference.

The best evidence comes from laboratory and animal research on how the small intestine absorbs biotin. Biotin is pulled into gut cells by a carrier protein that also moves pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). Studies on intestinal tissue exposed to alcohol, and in animals fed alcohol over long periods, have found that alcohol reduces the activity of this carrier, so less biotin gets in. Older studies in people with long-term alcohol dependence have also reported lower blood biotin levels than in people who don't drink heavily. The NIH fact sheet lists people with chronic alcohol exposure as one of the groups at higher risk of low biotin status.

Several things probably work together in heavy drinkers:

- **Lower absorption.** Alcohol interferes with the carrier that moves biotin across the gut wall.
- **Less biotin in the diet.** When alcohol makes up a large share of daily calories, there is less room for the foods that supply biotin, like eggs, meat, fish, nuts, seeds, and some vegetables.
- **Liver changes.** The liver stores and handles many vitamins. Alcohol-related liver damage can affect how well it does that.

Even so, true biotin deficiency is rare. Biotin is found in many foods, the body needs only a small amount, and bacteria in the gut make some too, though how much of that you actually absorb is still debated. Among the B vitamins, alcohol hits **thiamine (B1) and folate** much harder than biotin, and those are the ones doctors usually worry about first in people who drink heavily. Our guide to [vitamins depleted by alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamins-depleted-by-alcohol) ranks the main ones by how much alcohol affects them.

### What about the egg whites in cocktails?

This is a fun one. Raw egg whites contain a protein called **avidin** that binds tightly to biotin and stops you absorbing it. The classic way to give someone biotin deficiency, in older medical literature, was a diet with lots of raw egg whites over a long period.

Some cocktails, like the whiskey sour, pisco sour, and gin fizz, use a raw egg white for foam. A few of these on a night out won't affect your biotin status. You would need to eat raw egg whites regularly, in fairly large amounts, for weeks to months. Cooking destroys avidin, and cooked eggs (especially the yolks) are actually a good source of biotin. So if you like an egg-white sour now and then, it's not a nutrition concern. (The more relevant raw-egg risk is salmonella, which is why many bars use pasteurized whites.)

### Signs of low biotin

Because deficiency is uncommon, most people with these symptoms have a different cause. But it helps to know what doctors look for. Signs of biotin deficiency include:

- Thinning hair, sometimes with loss of hair color
- A red, scaly rash around the eyes, nose, mouth, and groin
- Red, irritated eyes (conjunctivitis)
- Brittle nails
- Tiredness, low mood, or lethargy
- Numbness, tingling, or burning in the hands and feet

Several of these overlap with problems that heavy drinking can cause by other routes, including low thiamine, low zinc, liver disease, and nerve damage from alcohol itself. That's why self-diagnosing from a symptom list doesn't work well here. If you have these signs and drink regularly, a doctor can run tests and find the real cause.

## The Lab Test Problem: Why Biotin Users Need to Speak Up

This is the most important section of this guide, and it's the part almost no one knows about.

Many common blood tests use a chemistry system built around the strong natural bond between biotin and a protein called streptavidin. When there is a lot of extra biotin in your blood, it can get in the way of that system and make results come out **falsely high or falsely low**, depending on how the test is designed.

The US Food and Drug Administration issued a safety warning about this in 2017 and updated it in 2019. The FDA said it had received reports of incorrect lab results linked to biotin, including at least one death, and that high biotin levels can cause falsely low results on some **troponin** tests. Troponin is the main blood test hospitals use to tell whether someone is having a heart attack. A falsely low result could mean a real heart attack gets missed.

Other tests that can be affected include:

- **Thyroid tests.** Biotin can make results look like an overactive thyroid when your thyroid is normal, or hide a real problem.
- **Some hormone tests**, including tests for vitamin D, cortisol, and reproductive hormones.
- **Some pregnancy tests** done in the lab.

The doses in a standard multivitamin (usually around 30 mcg) are unlikely to cause trouble. The concern is mostly with the high doses found in hair, skin, and nail supplements, which often contain 5,000 mcg or 10,000 mcg (5 or 10 mg) per serving. That's hundreds of times more than the amount adults need each day.

### Why this matters for people who drink

You might wonder what this has to do with alcohol. Two things:

**First, drinking is a common reason people end up getting blood work they didn't plan for.** A pounding heart, chest tightness, or palpitations after a heavy night out sends a lot of people to urgent care or the emergency room. Alcohol can trigger heart rhythm problems in some people, a pattern sometimes called "holiday heart." That's exactly the situation where a doctor orders a troponin test. If you're taking high-dose biotin, tell the staff. They may choose a different test or interpret the result with care. Our guide to [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains when a fast heartbeat is a hangover symptom and when it needs urgent care.

**Second, people who drink regularly often get liver tests.** Standard liver enzyme tests are not usually the ones affected by biotin, but people who get liver panels often get thyroid and other tests at the same time. It's simpler to tell your doctor about every supplement you take.

### What to do if you take biotin

- **Tell your doctor and the lab** that you take biotin before any blood test, and say how much.
- **Ask whether to pause it.** Many labs and doctors suggest stopping high-dose biotin for a few days before planned blood work. How long depends on the dose and the test, so follow your doctor's or the lab's advice rather than a fixed number.
- **Check your labels.** Biotin hides in multivitamins, prenatal vitamins, B-complex products, and "beauty" gummies. Add up every source.
- **In an emergency, say it out loud.** If you go to the ER with chest pain or a racing heart, mention the biotin along with what you drank. It takes ten seconds and can change how your results are read.

## Does Biotin Help With a Hangover?

There is no good evidence that biotin relieves or prevents a hangover.

A hangover comes from a mix of things: the after-effects of alcohol on sleep, dehydration and lost fluids, irritation of the stomach, a low-grade inflammatory response, the build-up of a toxic breakdown product called acetaldehyde, and, in some drinks, extra compounds called congeners. One night of drinking doesn't drain your biotin stores, and taking extra biotin doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol or acetaldehyde.

Biotin does turn up in plenty of hangover and "morning after" products, usually as part of a B-complex blend. If you feel better after one of those, the more likely reasons are the water you took it with, the electrolytes or sugar in the drink, the caffeine some contain, or simply the time passing. Our article on [B-complex and alcohol](/never-hungover/b-complex-and-alcohol) covers which B vitamins drinking actually affects and whether a B-complex is worth taking if you drink regularly.

If you want to feel better the morning after, the steps with the best support are dull but effective:

- Drink water between alcoholic drinks and before bed.
- Eat a real meal before and during drinking.
- Choose lighter, clearer drinks if you notice darker ones hit you harder.
- Protect your sleep, since alcohol already cuts sleep quality.
- Drink less, or drink more slowly.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each step and the evidence behind it.

## Biotin, Alcohol, and Hair Loss

A lot of people searching "biotin and alcohol" are really asking a hair question: *Is drinking making my hair thin, and will biotin fix it?*

### Can alcohol affect your hair?

Not usually directly, but it can contribute in a few indirect ways. Heavy drinking can lower your intake and absorption of nutrients that hair depends on, including protein, iron, zinc, and some B vitamins. It disrupts sleep. It can raise stress hormones. And a period of heavy drinking, illness, or major stress can push more hair follicles into their resting phase at once, which shows up as extra shedding a few months later. Doctors call that pattern telogen effluvium, and it usually recovers once the trigger is gone.

For a social drinker, alcohol is rarely the main cause of hair loss. Genetics, hormones, thyroid problems, iron deficiency, and stress are far more common culprits. Our guide on whether [alcohol causes hair loss](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-hair-loss) goes into the details.

### Will biotin help?

Probably not, unless you're actually low in biotin. A 2017 review in the journal *Skin Appendage Disorders* looked at the published cases where biotin was used for hair and nail problems. It found that the people who improved generally had an underlying cause of low biotin or a specific condition, and it concluded there wasn't good evidence to support biotin for hair loss in healthy people with normal levels. Because true deficiency is rare, most people taking biotin for hair are taking a vitamin they already have enough of.

For nails, the picture is a little more hopeful but still weak. A few small, older studies reported firmer nails in people with brittle nails who took biotin, but they were small and not well controlled. Biotin is cheap and generally well tolerated, so some dermatologists don't object to a trial for brittle nails. Just keep expectations modest and remember the lab test issue.

### A better approach if you think drinking is affecting your hair

- **Get the common causes checked.** Iron and ferritin, thyroid, and vitamin D are reasonable blood tests to ask about. (And tell the lab about your biotin first.)
- **Look at the pattern.** Sudden shedding a few months after a stressful or hard-drinking stretch often settles on its own once things calm down.
- **Cut back for a few months.** If alcohol is a factor, a sustained break gives you a real test of whether it matters for you.
- **See a doctor or dermatologist** for patchy loss, bald spots, a receding hairline, or shedding that lasts more than a few months.

## Biotin, Alcohol, and Skin

Biotin is also marketed for skin, and some people take it hoping to offset the dull, puffy, or dry skin that can follow a night of drinking. The facial puffiness and redness after drinking come mostly from fluid shifts, widened blood vessels, salty food, poor sleep, and, in some people, a reaction to acetaldehyde. Biotin doesn't address any of those. Our guides to [face bloating after drinking](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) and [itchy skin after drinking](/never-hungover/itchy-skin-after-drinking) cover what actually helps.

One more point: some people report breakouts while taking high-dose biotin. This hasn't been well studied, and the evidence is mostly anecdotal. One common theory is that large doses of biotin may compete with pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) for absorption, since both use the same carrier, but there is no good evidence for this yet. If your skin gets worse after starting a high-dose biotin product, it's reasonable to stop and see whether it clears.

## Biotin, Seizure Medications, and Alcohol

A few older seizure medications, including **carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, and primidone**, can lower biotin levels with long-term use. They speed up how fast the body breaks biotin down and may reduce absorption. These same drugs have their own serious issues with alcohol: alcohol can add to their drowsiness and dizziness, and heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal can make seizures more likely.

If you take any of these medicines, talk to your doctor before drinking at all, and ask whether a biotin supplement or a blood test makes sense. Don't stop or change a seizure medication on your own.

## How Much Biotin Do You Actually Need?

The amount adults need is small. The NIH sets an **Adequate Intake of 30 mcg a day** for adults, 30 mcg during pregnancy, and 35 mcg while breastfeeding. An Adequate Intake is used when there isn't enough data to set a precise requirement, and it reflects the amount that appears to keep healthy people well supplied.

Most people get that from food without trying. Good sources include:

- Cooked eggs, especially the yolk
- Liver and other organ meats
- Salmon and other fish
- Meat and poultry
- Nuts and seeds, such as almonds and sunflower seeds
- Sweet potatoes and some other vegetables

There is no special biotin dose for people who drink. If you drink moderately and eat a varied diet, you don't need a supplement. If you drink heavily, the bigger nutritional priorities are usually thiamine and folate, along with a broad improvement in diet. Many doctors recommend a basic multivitamin or a B-complex for people who drink heavily, which covers biotin at sensible doses without the very high amounts found in hair products. Our guide to [multivitamins and alcohol](/never-hungover/multivitamin-and-alcohol) covers when one is worth taking.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You don't need to worry about biotin and alcohol if you're a healthy adult who drinks socially. Take more care if you:

- **Take high-dose biotin and have blood tests coming up**, or have heart or thyroid conditions that need regular monitoring.
- **Drink heavily most days.** Biotin is one of many nutrients that can run low, and a doctor can check for the more common deficiencies too.
- **Take carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, or primidone.** Ask your doctor about both alcohol and biotin.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** Biotin needs may be slightly higher, and alcohol is best avoided in pregnancy.
- **Have a rare inherited condition called biotinidase deficiency**, which is usually picked up through newborn screening and treated with biotin under a doctor's care.

## When to See a Doctor

Most questions about biotin and alcohol aren't urgent. But some symptoms deserve a proper check rather than another supplement:

- **Get emergency care right away (call 911)** for chest pain or pressure, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, fainting, or severe shortness of breath, whether or not you've been drinking. Tell the staff you take biotin.
- **See a doctor soon** for numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet, trouble with balance, a red scaly rash around your eyes, nose, or mouth, or hair loss that is sudden, patchy, or lasts more than a few months.
- **Talk to your doctor** if you notice you're drinking most days and feeling run down, or if you've been told your liver tests are abnormal. A blood test can show whether you're low in key nutrients and how your liver is doing.

## Where DHM Fits In

Biotin doesn't do anything about alcohol itself. If your real goal is to feel better after drinking and give your body less to recover from, the most effective step is still drinking less and drinking slower, with food and water along the way.

Some people also add **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that DHM reliably prevents hangovers, and it isn't a substitute for drinking sensibly. It doesn't affect biotin, and it has no known effect on the blood tests biotin can interfere with. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any new supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Biotin and alcohol are safe together. There's no known dangerous interaction.
- Long-term heavy drinking can lower biotin absorption, but true deficiency is rare, and thiamine and folate are bigger concerns for heavy drinkers.
- There is no good evidence that biotin helps a hangover or reverses alcohol's effects on hair or skin.
- High-dose biotin can distort blood tests, including the troponin test used to diagnose heart attacks. Tell your doctor, the lab, and emergency staff that you take it.
- The egg white in a whiskey sour won't affect your biotin.
- If you're worried about your hair, skin, or energy and you drink regularly, a doctor's check and cutting back on alcohol will usually do more than any supplement.

For how this fits with other supplements people take around drinking, see our overview of [the vitamins and minerals alcohol depletes](/never-hungover/vitamins-depleted-by-alcohol) and our [milk thistle and alcohol](/never-hungover/milk-thistle-and-alcohol) guide.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take biotin and drink alcohol?**

Yes. There's no known dangerous interaction between biotin and alcohol. Biotin doesn't change your blood alcohol level, doesn't cause drowsiness, and isn't processed by the same liver pathways as alcohol. You don't need to skip your biotin or multivitamin on days you drink. The main caution is unrelated to alcohol itself: high-dose biotin can interfere with some blood tests, so tell your doctor and the lab you take it.

**Does alcohol deplete biotin?**

Long-term heavy drinking can lower biotin levels. Research in animals and intestinal tissue shows alcohol reduces the activity of the carrier that moves biotin across the gut wall, and older studies found lower blood biotin in people with long-term alcohol dependence. Occasional or moderate drinking is unlikely to make a meaningful difference. Thiamine and folate are affected much more than biotin.

**Does biotin help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that biotin relieves or prevents a hangover. One night of drinking doesn't drain your biotin, and extra biotin doesn't speed up how your body clears alcohol or acetaldehyde. If a hangover product with B vitamins seems to help, the water, electrolytes, sugar, or caffeine in it are more likely reasons.

**Will biotin stop hair loss from drinking?**

Probably not, unless you're actually low in biotin, which is uncommon. Reviews of the evidence have found little support for biotin in people with normal levels. Heavy drinking can contribute to hair shedding through poor nutrition, stress, and poor sleep, so cutting back and getting iron, thyroid, and vitamin D checked are more useful steps. See a doctor for sudden, patchy, or lasting hair loss.

**Can biotin affect blood tests?**

Yes. High-dose biotin can make some lab tests read falsely high or falsely low. The FDA has warned that it can cause falsely low troponin results, which could lead to a missed heart attack, and it can also distort thyroid and some hormone tests. The risk is mostly with the 5,000 to 10,000 mcg doses in hair and nail supplements. Tell your doctor and the lab before any blood test, and mention it in the ER.

**Do egg white cocktails block biotin?**

Not in any way that matters. Raw egg white contains avidin, a protein that binds biotin, but you'd need to eat raw egg whites regularly and in large amounts for weeks or months to become deficient. An occasional whiskey sour or pisco sour won't affect your biotin status. Cooking destroys avidin, and cooked eggs are a good source of biotin.

**How much biotin should I take if I drink?**

There is no special dose for drinkers. The NIH Adequate Intake for adults is 30 mcg a day, which most people get from food like eggs, fish, meat, nuts, and seeds. If you drink heavily, a basic multivitamin or B-complex covers biotin along with the B vitamins alcohol affects more, like thiamine and folate. Ask your doctor before taking high-dose biotin, especially if you need regular blood work.

**Is it safe to take biotin the morning after drinking?**

Yes. It won't hurt, and it won't interact with any alcohol still in your system. It also won't do much for how you feel. Water, food, rest, and time are what help a hangover. If you're feeling chest pain or a racing heart and heading to get checked, tell the staff you take biotin so they can read your blood tests correctly.
